summary: Resized the mother dragon to match canon (broad-bodied, near a child's waist height, small for a dragon) in S003 and S096, removing the fishing-boat size and the wing twice Ekin's height.

spans: Ekin had been standing at the harbour stall for a full minute, turning the brass compass over in her palms, when the shadow fell across her.
It came from above and behind, fast and silent, and by the time she looked up, a dragon the size of a fishing boat had landed on the pier, its tail curling around the stall's post.
Its wings were folded like a grey cloak, its belly wide and pale, and it didn't roar or breathe fire at all.
It simply leaned down, its long neck stretching over her shoulder, and plucked the compass from her hands with two neat claws.
"Hey—that's mine!" Ekin grabbed at empty air.
The dragon's wing swept backward as it turned, knocking a stack of paper receipts off the stall and scattering them across the wet stone like startled gulls.
The dragon paid no attention to any of it.
It lifted the compass to its eye, tilted its head as if admiring the shine, and then launched itself off the pier with three powerful wingbeats.
The dragon rose, banked, and she lost it against the bright grey sky, her heart hammering.
She spun around, searching the rooftops, the masts, the breakwater—then a voice behind her said, "You're going the wrong way.
A girl her own age stood there, arms crossed, dark hair whipping in the wind.
Ekin had seen her around the harbour before but had never spoken to her.
"It went toward the cliffs," Ekin said.
"It went toward the lighthouse." The girl pointed.
High on the old lighthouse's seaward face, in a broken upper window, something flashed—brief, brass-bright, gone.
"He used to take me out along the coast with it.
I was just looking at it.
Yes." The girl was already walking, briskly, toward the path that climbed the headland.
Ekin hesitated for one breath, then ran to catch up.
"I'm Duru, by the way," the girl said, without looking back.
The path ran above the tide line, dry and sheltered, winding along the shoulder of the headland toward the lighthouse.
Below it, the shore was a chaos of wet stone and rock pools, and it looked shorter—Ekin could see the lighthouse directly across the jumble of rocks.
"The shore's where the waves will be in half an hour." Duru nodded at the horizon, where a wall of dark cloud had begun to lean against the sky.
The wind had picked up since the harbour, and whitecaps were showing far out.
"Look at the tide line on those rocks.
The water reaches there when it blows from the west.
That's where we're standing if we go down."
The stain was high—higher than she'd guessed.
She felt a small, stubborn itch to argue anyway, just because Duru had said it like a teacher, but the wind chose that moment to shove her sideways, and she decided the path was fine.
They climbed in a rattling silence broken by Duru pointing things out despite herself: the old anchor chain half-buried in the grass, the hollow where fishermen used to dry their nets.
"Nobody's been up to the lighthouse in years," Duru said.
It stood at the base of the tower, a heavy iron-banded thing, ajar for the first time in what looked like a very long while.
Sand and gull feathers had drifted across the threshold.
A smell came out of the dark inside—salt, and something warmer, like sun-baked stone.
Duru stopped with her hand on the door.
"I always wanted to see inside," she admitted, quietly, as if confessing to something.
"Then let's go," Ekin said, and slipped past her through the opening.
The stairs inside spiralled up through cold air and drifting light.
Near the top, daylight poured through a wide broken window, and the tower opened into a broad room—dry, bright, littered with old machinery and dust.
And in the far corner, heaped against the wall beneath the broken glass, was the dragon.
The room was bigger than Ekin had expected, and stranger.
The wind moaned through the broken window in low, shifting notes, like someone humming behind a closed door.
The glass in the remaining panes had gone cloudy with salt, so the light came through thick and pearly.

Old winch gears stood along one wall under shrouds of dust, and every bright thing in the room had been collected into one corner: a brass ship's bell, a lantern with a polished reflector, a handful of doorknobs, a tin lid, a fisherman's lucky coin, all piled in a wide, shallow nest of dried grass and rope ends.
And on top of the pile, unmistakable, lay the compass.
There it was—her grandfather's compass, dented at the edge where she'd once dropped it, the needle casing fogged with salt from a hundred mornings at the shore.
The dragon was curled around the nest, its body filling the whole corner, its head resting on its forelegs.
"Because of that." Duru pointed, very slightly, with her chin.
Ekin followed her look and saw it: a small shape at the edge of the nest, hardly bigger than a cat, peering out from behind its mother's wing.
A hatchling—sleek, grey-green, with enormous eyes and a damp, unfinished look about it, the way kittens have.
It was nudging at the tin lid with its nose, utterly absorbed.
"And the mother is between us and the whole room," Duru said.
We don't walk up to a dragon's nest and grab things, even if—"
But Ekin had already stopped listening, because one of the dragon's wings had shifted, just an inch, and beneath it she could see the compass's brass edge catching the pearly light.
Every hiss and rustle from the mother felt aimed at her, like a dare.
Duru wasn't the boss of this.
She noticed, distantly, a narrow doorway in the far wall, and a staircase corkscrewing down into the dark of the tower's lower floor.
From somewhere below came the sound of waves—close, hollow, drumming against stone.
The sea was already speaking through the building.
She crossed the room in six quick strides and reached for the compass.
The mother came off the nest like a door slamming.
One wing flared wide, twice Ekin's height, and the hiss that came out of the animal was pure fury and pure warning all at once, and Ekin stumbled backward, her hand never touching the brass.

The compass, knocked by the edge of the wing, rolled off the nest, bounced once on the stone floor, and slid—spinning, wobbling—straight across the room and down through the narrow doorway, clattering away down the corkscrew stairs into the dark.
The hatchling shrieked, a sound like a kettle coming to the boil, and bolted.
Ekin saw it go—saw it pour itself down the same narrow staircase in a tumble of claws and tail, vanishing into the lower dark after a hiding place only it knew.
The mother lunged after it, got her head and shoulders into the stairwell, and jammed.
Her chest was simply too broad for the turning stair.
She shoved, wings battering the doorframe, dust and grit raining down, and got nowhere.
She was stuck, half-in, half-out, hissing down into the dark where her baby had gone.
She had not moved from her spot, and her voice was tight.
Ekin leaned into the stairwell, peering down the spiral.

Far below, in the gloom of the lower room, she could see the compass lying on the stone floor near the seaward wall—and beyond the compass, a wide opening in that wall, closed by a fixed iron grille, and beyond the grille, the sea.
The waves were no longer drumming from a distance.
White water surged against the bars, and spray was already spitting through the gaps, wetting the floor in a growing, creeping sheet.
A swell surged harder than the rest.
Water foamed through the grille, rushed across the floor, and dragged the compass with it.
Ekin watched it scrape over the stone, catch for one horrible half-second on the bars, and then slide through the gap and out, into the grey churn, gone.
Below, the hatchling scrambled up onto a dry stone ledge near the foot of the stairs, out of the water's reach, and pressed itself there, shivering, its eyes two dots of reflected white.
The mother, wedged in the stairwell above them, hissed down into the dark at her baby, at the water, at everything, and could do nothing at all.
For a long moment Ekin couldn't look away from the grille.
The compass was out there, somewhere under the grey water, and her whole body wanted to run down those stairs and find some way—any way—to get it back.
This whole floor will be under it."
Some stubborn part of her refused to accept it, and that part was shouting down every other thought.
Then the hatchling cried out again—small, high, desperate—from its ledge, and the mother thrashed against the doorframe above, and Ekin felt something in her chest turn over.
Her voice came out flat and strange.
It's down there because of me.
The compass too—if I hadn't lunged at it—"
She didn't soften it and she didn't pile on.
She just said it, and then she said: "So what are you going to do?"
Ekin looked at the stairs, at the hatchling on its ledge, at the water climbing the floor below in slow, glittering advances.
She thought about the dry room above, and the open door, and the path home, and how easy it would be to just leave.
The compass was lost either way.
Duru's jaw was set and her eyes were angry, and she stayed.
"The ledge near the bottom is still dry," she said.
"If it comes to the stairs, we can get it up."
The top steps were dry; the water had not reached them.
She crouched on the lowest dry step, opened her jacket, and held it out—not toward the hatchling, not chasing it, just open, like a nest, like a suggestion.
The hatchling pressed itself back against the stone, hissing, its whole small body shaking.
I'm the one who scared you.
Behind and above her, Duru stood one step higher, watching, calling the water level: "Still dry.
Coming up on the left—move your foot." Her voice steadied Ekin more than she could say.
The swell came, and the ledge began to vanish, and the hatchling had nowhere left to retreat except toward the stairs—toward Ekin.
She waited, jacket open, heart pounding, and the wave decided for all of them: the hatchling sprang, landed against her chest, and burrowed into the jacket like it had always lived there.
Ekin rose, one hand cupping the small warm weight, and climbed.
Duru took her arm at the turn, steadied her at the half-landing, and pulled her through the doorway into the dry light of the upper room.
The mother was already off the stairwell, wings wide, and Ekin walked straight to her and knelt and let the hatchling tumble out of her jacket onto the nest.
The mother's head came down over her baby.
The hiss this time was low, and brief, and ended.
Ekin backed away, slowly, and the dragon let her.
She stood beside Duru in the middle of the room, wind howling through the broken window, and watched as the mother folded herself around the hatchling, one great wing drawing over it like a roof.
It did not nod or thank them.
It did not reach into the nest and bring out a gift, and Ekin understood, in a way that settled into her bones, that it never would.
The hatchling peeked out from under the wing once, looked at her with its enormous eyes, and tucked itself back in.
They went down the spiral stairs inside the tower, past the door they'd come through, and out into the wind.
The coast path was still dry, still sheltered, though the sea below had climbed to its dark stain on the rocks and the rain was starting in slanting sheets.
At the fork where the path bent inland, she called back, "This way—the low ground floods," and Ekin followed without a word, without arguing, without even feeling the usual itch to.
It was just that Duru was right, and Ekin could admit it now.
They walked a while in the rain's soft noise.
Duru didn't mock her about the compass, and somehow that was worse and better than teasing all at once.
"It's really gone," Ekin said at last.
"I keep thinking I'll see it on the beach tomorrow.
Ekin's hand went to her pocket, where the compass's cord still hung—a braided cord with nothing on the end of it now.
She wound it around her fingers, once, twice, feeling the emptiness of it, and found that she didn't want to hide it or lie about what had happened to it.
She would tell her grandfather the truth.
The dragon took it, and then I lost it, and then I left it in the sea, and here's what came back instead of it.
Her fingers tightened on the empty cord.
"Duru," she said, catching up, falling into step beside her.
How long has it been open?"
Duru glanced at her, and something shifted in her face—a small, careful curiosity, finally out in the open.
"Because I want to go back," Ekin said.
Ahead, the path curved down toward the harbour lights, and the rain kept falling, and neither of them said anything else for a while—but they walked the whole way together.

approved_plan.reader_promise:
12 yaş okuru; fantastik kıyı macerası; önce İngilizce yazım için 1.400–1.800
kelimelik hedef önerisi. Merak, sürtüşmeli ortaklık ve kaybı inkâr etmeyen bir son.
Başlangıç sorusu: Ekin dedesinin pusulasını geri alabilecek mi? Asıl çatışma:
Ekin kendi hatası ortaya çıktığında sorumluluk alabilecek mi?

Pusula büyülü değildir. Hazine, kehanet veya büyük Saga sırrı açıklamaz. Bu tek
bölümün kendi macerası kapanır; devam bölümü gerektiren yapay cliffhanger yoktur.
approved_plan.mock_context:
**Ekin:** On iki yaşında bir kız. Meraklı, çabuk karar veriyor; kendisine yol
gösterilmesini küçümsenmek gibi algılıyor. Dedesiyle yaptığı kıyı gezilerinden
kalan pirinç pusula, o gezileri tek başına da yapabileceğine dair kişisel bir
hatıra. Dedenin öldüğü varsayılmayacak; hikâye bir yas anlatısına dönüştürülmeyecek.

**Duru:** Ekin'in yaşıtı. Eski fenerin yolunu biliyor. Ekin'e hizmet eden kusursuz
yardımcı değil: laf sokuyor, merakını bazen saklıyor, kendi fikrinin dinlenmesini
istiyor. Fenerin kapısı uzun süredir ilk kez açık olduğu için o da içeri girmek
istiyor. Ortaklıklarının başlangıç nedeni yalnızca Ekin'e iyilik etmek değil.

**Anne deniz ejderhası:** Çocukların beline yaklaşan, geniş gövdeli bir hayvan;
diğer ejderhalara göre küçük. Uçabilir, küçük bir metal nesneyi taşıyabilir.
Konuşmaz, büyü yapmaz, insan niyetini okuyamaz. Yuvaya parlak eşyalar taşır.
İnsanlara saldırma amacı yok; yaklaşanı kanat açıp tıslayarak uzaklaştırır.

**Yavru:** Kedi büyüklüğünde, koşabilir ve dar aralıklara girebilir; henüz
uçamaz. Düşüp yaralanması veya grafik acı tasviri yok. Korktuğunda dar, karanlık
bir yere saklanma davranışı var. Annenin ganimetleriyle ilgilenmesi keşifte görülür.

**Başlangıç eşyaları:** Ekin'in pusulası ve ceketi; Duru'nun sıradan giysileri.
Sonradan ip, kanca, kesici alet, özel ışık veya kurtarma ekipmanı belirmeyecek.
approved_plan.setting_and_hazards:
Fener ana karaya bağlı bir burunda. Limandan üst kapıya çıkan kıyı patikası su
basma çizgisinin üstünde; bir ada geçidi, kopacak köprü veya gizli ikinci yol yok.
Gidişte Duru korunaklı patikayı gösterir. Fırtına yaklaşır ama başlangıçta dalgalar
alt deniz duvarına dahi ulaşmaz; çocuklar kısa bir ziyaret yapabileceklerini sanır.

Üst giriş odası kuru ve gün ışığı alıyor. Anne burada, geniş kırık pencereden
ulaşabildiği köşede yuva kurmuş. Odanın bir kenarından alt bakım odasına dar,
dönüşlü bir insan merdiveni iner. Çocuklar geçebilir; annenin geniş göğsü dönüşten
geçemez. Bu engel sahnede annenin gerçekten denemesiyle görünür; sonradan ilan
edilen bir tür kuralı değildir.

Alt bakım odasının denize bakan açıklığında sabit bir demir ızgara vardır. Su
ve küçük nesneler geçebilir; anne dışarıdan buraya giremez. Fırtınada dalgalar
bu açıklıktan içeri dolar. İç merdiven üstteki kuru odaya çıkar ve sağlam kalır.
Çocuklar yüzmeye, dalmaya veya görünmeyen zeminde ilerlemeyecek.

Tehlike tüm binanın birden batması değil: alt odanın yavru için hızla güvensiz
olması, görüşü bozan su ve dışarıdaki rüzgârın artmasıdır. Fırtına aniden durmaz;
sonda annenin uçması gerekmeyecek. Anne ve yavru kuru üst odada buluşur.

scenes.title: Limandaki hırsızlık
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin pusulaya bakarken ejderha onu kapar. Hayvanın kanadı tezgâhtaki hafif
kâğıtları savurur; hırsızlık kısa, canlı bir sahnedir. Ekin peşinden koşar.
Duru onun yanlış yöne gittiğini söyleyip fenerin penceresindeki parıltıyı gösterir.
scenes.required_end_state: Pusula anne ejderhada; iki çocuk limanda, birlikte gitmeye karar verir.

scenes.title: İstemeden ortaklık
scenes.approved_action:
Duru kıyı patikasını seçer. Ekin daha kısa gördüğü taşlık kıyıya yönelmek ister;
Duru dalgaların oraya kadar çıkacağını gösterir. Ekin onun yolunu isteksizce kabul
eder. Aralarında birinin sürekli haklı olduğu ders sahnesi değil, karşılıklı
iğnelemeler ve fener hakkında ortak merak vardır. Açık kapıdan içeri girerler.
scenes.required_end_state: İkisi kuru üst odada. Geri dönüş yolu okura gösterilmiş olur.

scenes.title: Hırsızın evi
scenes.approved_action:
Rüzgârın boş fenerde çıkardığı sesleri, tuzla matlaşmış camları ve yuvaya taşınmış
ufak parlak eşyaları keşfederler. Ekin pusulayı görür. Duru bir yavru fark eder
ve yaklaşmadan önce beklemelerini ister. Ekin her tıslamayı pusulasına karşı
bir meydan okuma gibi algılar; Duru'nun uyarısını emir sayar.

Dar merdiven ağzı ve alt odanın ızgarasından duyulan dalga sesi bu sahnede gösterilir.
Çıkıştaki kapı ve dönüş yolu kapanmaz. Anne çocuklarla yuvanın arasında durur.
scenes.required_end_state: Herkes üst odada, pusula yuvanın yanında. Yavru ile inişin yeri belli.

scenes.title: Ekin'in hatası
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin pusulaya hızla uzanır. Anne kanadını açarak onu uzaklaştırır. Pusula yuvanın
kenarından yuvarlanıp merdivenden alt odaya gider. Ürken yavru da merdivenin altına
kaçar; çocuklar onun nereye gittiğini görür. Anne peşinden inmeye çalışır ama dar
dönüşte kalır. Duru çocuğu veya hayvanı iterek sorunu büyütmez.

Ekin merdivenden bakarken bir dalga pusulayı ızgaranın aralığından denize sürükler.
Yavru alt basamakların yakınındaki kuru taş çıkıntıya çekilir. Suyu görürler;
tehlike anlatıcının soyut uyarısıyla değil sahnedeki değişimle belirginleşir.
scenes.required_end_state:
Pusula denizde ve erişilemiyor. Anne üstte; yavru altta. Çocuklar
merdivenin kuru bölümünde. Fenerin üst çıkışı hâlâ kullanılabilir.

scenes.title: Geri dönmek yerine sorumluluk almak
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin önce gözünü pusulanın kaybolduğu ızgaradan ayıramaz. Duru gitmeleri gerektiğini
söyler; ardından yavrunun su yükseldikçe geri çekildiğini görürler. Ekin hayvanı
kendisinin ürküttüğünü kabul eder ve Duru'dan yardım ister. Duru da ona kızgın
olmasına rağmen kalır. Karar: Kendi kaybına kapanıp ayrılmak mı, yol açtığı
tehlikeyi gidermek için güvenli kalan kısa fırsatı kullanmak mı?

Ekin kuru kalan basamakta çömelip ceketini açar. Yavrunun arkasına geçmez veya
onu suya doğru kovalamaz. Duru aynı merdivende bir üst basamakta durur; görüşü
izler ve Ekin'in ceketle aldığı yavruyu yukarı aktarırken destek olur. Yavru
ulaşılabilir taş çıkıntıdadır; uçuruma atlama, suya dalma veya yeni büyü yoktur.
Ekin ardından aynı basamaklardan çıkar. Yazım bu basit eylemi sayfalar süren bir
mekanik bulmacaya çevirmemeli; gerilim Ekin'in tereddüdü ve hayvanın korkusundadır.
scenes.required_end_state: Çocuklar ve yavru kuru üst odada; anneyle buluşurlar. Pusula hâlâ kayıp.

scenes.title: Pusulasız dönüş
scenes.approved_action:
Ekin yavruyu annesinin yanına bırakır. Anne kanadını yavrunun üstüne kapatır;
konuşup teşekkür etmez, pusulayı veya başka bir armağanı geri vermez. Duru ile
Ekin gidişte gördüğümüz patikadan eve döner. Ekin bu kez Duru'nun yönlendirmesini
itiraz etmeden dinler; Duru da kaybıyla alay etmez.
scenes.required_end_state:
Ekin pusulaya olanları saklamamaya karar verir. Son görüntü: cebindeki boş pusula
kordonunu parmaklarıyla çevirirken Duru'ya yetişmesi. Mutlu bir kahkaha her şeyi
silmez; okur hem kaybı hem aralarındaki değişimi hisseder. Tamamlanan macera
yalnızca 'bir ders öğrendi' cümlesiyle özetlenmez.

approved_plan.preserved_outcomes:
- Pusulayı anne çalar; Ekin'in aceleciliği kaybı ve yavrunun korkup kaçmasını tetikler.
- Yavru altta kalır çünkü anne dar insan merdiveninden ve dış ızgaradan geçemez.
- Kurtarma kararını Ekin verir; Duru somut katkı sağlar. İkisi de yer değiştirmeden
  veya bir anda karşı tarafa belirmeden aynı merdiven üzerinden hareket eder.
- Pusula geri gelmez; yerine daha değerli ödül konmaz.
- Anne/yavru üstte güvendedir. Çocukların dönüşü gösterilir, fırtınanın bitmesi gerekmez.
- Hiçbir gizli güç, yetişkin kurtarıcı, açıklanmamış ekipman veya yeni yol çözüm olmaz.
- Yaşa uygun gerilim vardır; kanlı yaralanma, hayvan işkencesi ve didaktik final yoktur.
approved_plan.approved_clarifications:
Anneyle yavrunun fırtınada uçup uzaklaşması yerine kuru üst odada buluşması
öneriliyor. Pusula gerçekten erişilemez olduktan sonra sahte bir 'ikisini birden
alamaz' seçimi kurulmayacak. Ekin'in kararı kaybını kabul edip yol açtığı sorunu

findings.exact_text: a dragon the size of a fishing boat had landed on the pier
findings.reason: Canon says the mother is a broad-bodied animal approaching children's waist height, small compared to other dragons. A fishing-boat-sized dragon with a wing twice Ekin's height contradicts this. It also conflicts with the later claim that she is too broad for the stairs, since she is shown pushing into a narrow stairwell.
